This is part two of the crossover project. Part one is here and part three is here. A conference talk based on this work is now available here.

No one thinks about moving the starting or ending point of the bridge midway through construction. -Justin Cave

I had to move a bridge. -Anonymous1

Carl worked as a mechanical verification engineer: he tested oil rigs to see how much they vibrated. Humans work and live on oil rigs for long stretches of time, and if they vibrate too much it can be impossible to sleep. While rigs are designed to stay below the threshold, the design and the final version often diverge.

Currently, he was explaining how they find oil. After drilling a hole, he said, “you might also want to add other additives, like acid or hazelnut shells, but also-”

I stopped him. “Hazelnut shells?”

He smiled. “Your oil reservoir is not like a balloon full of oil. It’s more like a porous structure in the rock.” When drilling in, you might hit a sudden loss of pressure in the pipe. This is extremely dangerous as you don’t know if you’ve broken into the open ocean or have just hit a local void. In the latter case, digging further and suddenly hitting a high pressure area could destroy the pipe. By pumping in hazelnut shells they can gradually fill in small voids and test if they are still in the structure, gradually equalizing the pressure if they are.

According to Carl, oil companies are the biggest purchasers of hazelnut shells in Norway.

Debates about traditional versus software engineering revolve around what makes us different. The clichés here come from a different camp than the “what makes an engineer” clichés. The ways people try to define “engineering” often work to marginalize software. Differences like “we don’t have licenses” or “we’re not rigorous” are ways of saying that software is less prestigious, less “good” than traditional engineering. As we saw in the last essay, most of these don’t hold up, and the crossover engineers think the two jobs are much closer in nature than people who have only done one.

When people talk about the fundamental differences, in contrast, they’re usually not aiming to delegitimize software development. Rather, the implicit emphasis is on making software “special”. Making software something that can’t be understood by the narrow lens of engineering.

I see this as a defense mechanism. If software is so different from trad, then it’s okay for us to “not be engineers”. We can say that, sure, we aren’t planning upfront, but that’s because software requirements change so much faster than everywhere else. We don’t apply engineering because we shouldn’t be applying engineering. A good example of this is the NoEstimates movement: because estimates are difficult to make in software, supposedly unlike trad engineering, we should do away with them entirely.

There’s just one problem with this: as software engineers, we deeply misunderstand the nature of trad engineering. We are not special. Almost everything we think is unique about software appears in every other field of engineering. The upside of this is that—well, we are not special. Almost everything we think is awful about software is something everyone else struggles with, too.

The claimed differences

There’s a fallacy in comparing “trad”, which is an umbrella of different engineering disciplines, to software. Most arguments about engineering don’t go much beyond “software vs engineering”, or conflate “engineering” with civil engineering. All of the subfields are different, and the qualities of one don’t reflect on the qualities of others. After a few interviews, I settled on a set of “universal” differences to discuss:

  1. Traditional engineering is best done in a Waterfall style, while software is best done in an Agile one.
  2. Trad engineering is very predictable, while software is very unpredictable.
  3. Engineering is mostly about manufacture, while code is mostly about design, because “the code is the design”.
  4. Trad engineering is much more rigorous than software engineering is.
  5. Software moves much faster than traditional engineering does.

These aren’t all wrong. As we’ll see later, there are absolutely some differences between software and trad. But the majority of the differences are “wrong”, or at least lacking critical nuance.

Traditional is Waterfall, Software is Agile

If there’s one thing we think is uniquely software, it’s Agile.

As it’s told, Agile was a rejection of “Waterfall”, the old paradigm Winston Royce invented in 1970. Royce came up with the Waterfall model to mimic how “real” engineers built buildings. Waterfall says that you should do everything in a strict order, only progressing to the next stage of development when the current stage is completed. You only develop after you complete design, only test after you finish development, etc. This works for “real” engineering but utterly fails for software, where requirements change and often the customer doesn’t know what they want before you build it. So this is rejected by the Agile Manifesto in 2001, and everybody lived happily ever after.

Of course, this story is more fiction than fact. While Waterfall was a dominant model for some time, it was never quite as strict as we think it was today. Nor was it all that ubiquitous: most developers in the 70s and 80s were either working with an ad hoc plan or working in one of the many, many, many “incremental” models that were in fashion, like the Spiral Model and the V Model. Agile wasn’t a radical shift as much as a natural consequence of the trends at the time.

But all that is tangential to the core claim: software engineering is Agile, while trad engineering is Waterfall. And this, unsurprisingly, is a significant oversimplification.

It’s true that traditional engineers do a lot more upfront design and spend more time in dedicated testing than software engineers do. But this doesn’t mean they have Waterfall level rigidity, nor does it mean that our Agile is alien to them. Rather, spending a lot of time in phases is a natural consequence of the economic model. When iterations are longer and more expensive it makes more sense to spend more time planning them out. But people use “design” and “implement” in very different ways. When a civil engineer does a scale model, is that design or implementation? When an automotive engineer makes a full clay replica of a car to test its aesthetics and aerodynamics, is that design or implementation?

When it comes to things like making circuit boards, it’s pretty common for things not to work the first time. You have to do it again, and you have to send it out to the factory and do it again. You know it costs you another however many £1000 and another two weeks on the schedule. -Mike (electrical)

We see Agile-like innovations in every industry. Many tunnels today are built with Austrian Tunneling, which relies on iterative development and lots of room for improvisation. The Handbook of Industrial Engineering emphasises cross-collaboration and rapid client feedback. Even the most Waterfall form of engineering, civil engineering, gradually shifts to a more Agile-like process once construction starts. People need open communication and adaptation to deal with on-the-ground issues in building.

Why do we think software needs Agile and not Waterfall? Unpredictability. The Waterfall model only makes sense if we can accurately predict and estimate the obstacles inherent in our projects. Because software is unpredictable, the argument goes, we can’t use Waterfall. It could be that halfway through planning, we decide we need to start over. Is it any different for engineers? Is their work any more predictable, more certain than ours?

“Software is More Unpredictable”

*Laughter* -Dawn, Matt, Steve, Mike, Mat, Another Matt

Part of this misconception comes from us seeing the results of the engineering process, not the process itself. We don’t see the friction, the overruns, the delays that happen because someone built the wall one inch to the left, or when a critical supplier goes out of business. To assume that software is uniquely unpredictable is a special kind of arrogance.

Another part comes from how fast software seems to change. It feels like every year or two there is a new dominant framework or language that everybody’s trying to switch to. We expect that traditional engineering doesn’t have the same constant churn of tooling and paradigm. To an extent, it doesn’t. But less churn is not the same as no churn, and there are many other ways that things can become unpredictable. One chip designer, Steve, found this especially funny:

In the environment of software world, people are thinking ‘what’s the new JavaScript bundler of the month.’ In the hardware world, it’s ‘what can the silicon fab people do for us this month.’ If the foundry has new machinery to create chips, your plans change. Not as fast as libraries do, but still pretty fast. -Steve (electrical)

There are too many anecdotes to go into them all. Territory claims changing in the middle of construction, hardened procedures suddenly and permanently failing, new discoveries well into development. One person talked about how frustrating it is to start work on a bridge foundation, only to find that this particular soil freezes in a weird way that makes it liquefy too much in an earthquake. Back to the drawing board.

“The Code is the Design”

[Code is design] was a reaction to the people who think “Oh, if we just build a beautiful model in UML and then autogenerate all the code from UML then everything will be fine.”

That’s from Nick Coghlan. I was surprised when he reached out for an interview; I knew about him as a core CPython developer. Before that, though, he was a systems integration engineer for Boeing. “The diplomatic style of system architecture”, he called it. Boeing would have multiple independent systems- in his example, an airplane, air traffic control, and an antenna array. He had to work with all three teams to make sure they built compatible interfaces. Integration work, essentially. He saw “software is design” as the fundamental difference between his old job and his current one.

Others weren’t so sure. “From my view,” said one, “it was all design”, from the first schematics of the CPU to the final chips rolling out of the foundry. All of their time was spent on design, just like software. Construction was the easy part: just hand the design over to a foundry and get back completed chips.

Of course, the chips will come back flawed, which means a change in design. Design and construction aren’t nearly as disjoint as we software engineers think. Many of the mechanical engineers felt this strongly. The constructed product might show issues in the design, or it might show issues in the circumstances of construction. Mike, one mechanical engineer, called it “fettling”. Tweaking the design to deal with the slight imperfections of the construction process. Every construction changes the design, which changes the construction.

Beyond that, there’s another problem: “design” is not well specified. Are we talking about the architectural overview? The formal specification? The detailed blueprints? If the code is the design then what’s the formal specification of our code? For complex projects there are a lot of different kinds of design at a lot of different levels of detail. If you look at bridge plans, you see there are many layers of fractal detail.

I think this is another case where what we mean by design and construction really vary between different kinds of engineering. Yes, in civil engineering the construction phase takes the most time and money, but that’s civil engineering. And only certain kinds of civil engineering, too, the “bridges and buildings” work. The same kind of work on which we base our stereotypes.

I find myself having to explain that there are many aspects of civil engineering that you wouldn’t specifically consider. […] I tell people it refers to anything that you need to build the city. -Jen (civil)

Rigor

There’s like a 1,000,000 million times more checks and balances in software than in traditional engineering. […] Whenever someone’s tweeting about, like Excel horror stories *laughter* I have amazing Excel horror stories […] there’s days that I am shocked skyscrapers don’t fall over daily and planes don’t crash. -Mat

People say that trad engineering is a lot more rigorous than software. Trad engineers reason carefully from first principles rather than copy-paste. This is usually presented as a problem with software that we need to change to become “real” engineering. It’s also wrong.

First of all, any less rigor we have isn’t entirely cultural, because the essential nature of software makes it a viable tradeoff. Nick explained it as a difference in “validating assumptions”: “you reach a point with the easiest way to check if your assumption is right is to just go in and do it.” Software lets us gather empirical information more easily, which itself is a source of rigour.

But statements about rigor are predicated on the end results of software being different, that trad products are more coherent and less slapdash. That’s not true. For example, we keep much better records and use more comprehensive verification. I heard plenty of horror stories of critical information stored in Excel sheets and old filing cabinets, growing obsolete and corrupt. Plenty would kill to get the same kind of automated testing we treat as a given.

You can always add more brackets. -Carl

The Real Differences

So how is software different from everything else? A few ways.

Consistency

Software is entirely synthesized. It’s bounded entirely by logic. It doesn’t wear out like a spring, right? It just does what it’s supposed to do. The only thing that can actually go wrong is the specifications. The software was bad. -Nathan

Software is far more consistent than any other kind of engineering. We usually think of software as a giant mess, a haze of interdependencies and incompatible hardware, but we actually have it pretty nice. If I give you a sorting function, you can expect it to sort. You do not expect it to sort a given list of (nonpathological) numbers only 95% of the time. That would be ridiculous.

By contrast, let’s look at physical materials. In electrical engineering, a core component is the resistor: a wire that reduces the flow of current. Resistors are measured in ohms, and commodity off-the-shelf resistors can range from a single ohm to hundreds of millions of ohms. Many commodity resistors follow a color chart to make identifying the resistance easy:

So a band with green, blue, red will have 5600 ohms. Note the last band, though: that specifies the tolerance. The color code only describes the theoretical resistance: if the tolerance band is gold, that means the resistor can vary by up to 5%. If you have a batch of 100 of these resistors, some will be 5320 ohms, some will be 5880 ohms, and the only way to know which is which is to test each one individually. And this is to say nothing about wear and tear, or how resistance varies with temperature, etc.

This is the case of all physical materials. One of my favorite discoveries on the internet, well before I started this project, was the Fastenal labs page. Fastenal makes screws. One of their pages warns against using stainless steel screws on an aluminum plate.

Software engineering has nothing on that.

Velocity

The code is the spec for how the hardware should be running. In traditional engineering, we would have to do all that same work to share the spec, but then we have to wait and, like, let the fab or the machine shop finish building the damn thing. And then we’d have to sit there and install it either ourselves or hire somebody. And then we’d have to run testing on it for several weeks to see if it worked or not. -Matt (chemical)

This is irrefutable. We can change software much faster than anybody else can change their systems. Several engineers told me that changes had a quantifiable price tag: every time you needed to adjust something, you knew you were taking $5000 from the budget. Whereas I can change some code and run all the tests in seconds.

The closest I found to this in any other field was chemical engineering. “I’d go in the morning and look at what went wrong last night,” said Raja, a former chemical engineer. Something like a one minute turnover would be unheard of, and that’s already in the fastest field of non-software engineering.

This is the nature of our material. And it’s also why other engineering fields are progressively using more software by creating these design tools and simulations, engineers can prototype their ideas with software before implementing them.

There is also a darker side to this. Because software can iterate faster than trad, trad often relies on software to compensate for problems in physical equipment.

The software engineer is being squeezed by the rest of the team. They’re usually asked to save everyone’s bacon. If something is not quite working in the electronics or mechanics, often you can work around it with a software kludge. -Mike

And sometimes this reliance has catastrophic consequences. In 2019 over 300 people died in two 737 MAX airplane crashes. Investigation pinned this to a bug in the “Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System” (MCAS), one of the automated flight control systems. But Boeing only added MCAS in the first place to compensate for late-discovered issues with the plane’s aerodynamic profile. Rather than fix a trad issue with trad engineering, Boeing opted for the software kludge, and then people died.

Constraints

They have a [chip] time budget, you have a time budget, you say ‘I can’t quite make it. Do you have a little slop there? Can I get a fraction of a nanosecond?’ -Steve

One implicit undercurrent in all the interviews was the notion of constraint. There are hard physical limits that their products needed to obey. It has to be light enough, or strong enough, or resistant enough, or run cool enough. There is a known quantity they have to maximize or minimize.

Constraints are present in software, too. Code must fit in the memory of an embedded hardware device, the sensor needs a response in exactly 10 cycles, the API must stay under the rate limit. But constraints in software tend to be soft constraints. It is bad to go over them and the more we go over the worse it gets. We can slightly fudge the line if doing so will give us other benefits, like faster development time or simpler algorithms. In traditional engineering, most constraints are hard constraints. If the area of your box is a bit too wide then it won’t fit in the door.2

Sometimes this leads to unusual solutions. One time Carl’s team had to install a screw conveyor in an oil rig, then discovered it was just a couple inches too tall for the room. They couldn’t shrink the equipment, and they couldn’t raise the ceiling, since there were another four floors above it. The team’s solution? Cut a hole in the ceiling, put the equipment in, then put a box around the hole on the next floor so that nobody trips over it. Now that change is permanently part of the rig’s structure, something that has to be accommodated in every future change forever. And that leads to another difference: software engineers can undo their kludges. Trad engineers cannot.

Do the differences make us special?

While there are many ways we are different, there’s a difference between being “different” and being “special”. Yes, mechanical and electrical engineers don’t have to deal with the same security concerns we do. They also don’t have to deal with weather patterns to the same degree that civil engineers need to, and none of those three need to deal with the problems inherent in chemical engineering. Every field of engineering has unique challenges and software is no different.

But they are all much more similar than they are different. Every field values upfront, abstract thinking, tidy work, and a good kludge in just the right place. Every field faces shifting requirements and unknown unknowns. Every field is siloed from the others: we know as little about the work of mechanical engineers as chemical engineers do. Many times in my interviews, people asked what the other fields of engineering were like. Nobody ever gets a chance to leave their bubble.

And it’s a good thing that software isn’t special. It means that we can learn a lot on how to make software better from these other fields. And it means that they have a lot to learn from us. Because surprisingly, there are some ways that we are better at engineering than traditional engineers. Next time, we’ll cover what we can learn and what we can teach.

Part three, What Engineering Can Teach (and Learn from) Us, is available here. If you enjoyed these essays, I have a weekly newsletter and am on Twitter.

Thanks to Glenn Vanderburg, Chelsea Troy, Will Craft, and Dan Luu for feedback, and to all of the engineers whom I interviewed.

  2. Some software follows hard constraints, too: if the printer skips a bit then your document is ruined. But “real-time computing” makes up a small minority of the software space. [return]

Resistors are measured in ohms, and commodity off-the-shelf resistors can range from a single ohm to hundreds of millions of ohms. Many commodity resistors follow a color chart to make identifying the resistance easy: (source) So a band with green, blue, red will have 5600 ohms. Note the last band, though: that specifies the tolerance. The color code only describes the theoretical resistance: if the tolerance band is gold, that means the resistor can vary by up to 5%. If you have a batch of 100 of these resistors, some will be 5320 ohms, some will be 5880 ohms, and the only way to know which is which is to test each one individually. And this is to say nothing about wear and tear, or how resistance varies with temperature, etc. This is the case of all physical materials. One of my favorite discoveries on the internet, well before I started this project, was the Fastenal labs page. Fastenal makes screws. One of their pages warns against using stainless steel screws on an aluminum plate. Software engineering has nothing on that. Velocity The code is the spec for how the hardware should be running. In traditional engineering, we would have to do all that same work to share the spec, but then we have to wait and, like, let the fab or the machine shop finish building the damn thing. And then we’d have to sit there and install it either ourselves or hire somebody. And then we’d have to run testing on it for several weeks to see if it worked or not. -Matt (chemical) This is irrefutable. We can change software much faster than anybody else can change their systems. Several engineers told me that changes had a quantifiable price tag: every time you needed to adjust something, you knew you were taking $5000 from the budget. Whereas I can change some code and run all the tests in seconds. The closest I found to this in any other field was chemical engineering. “I’d go in the morning and look at what went wrong last night,” said Raja, a former chemical engineer. Something like a one minute turnover would be unheard of, and that’s already in the fastest field of non-software engineering. This is the nature of our material. And it’s also why other engineering fields are progressively using more software by creating these design tools and simulations, engineers can prototype their ideas with software before implementing them. There is also a darker side to this. Because software can iterate faster than trad, trad often relies on software to compensate for problems in physical equipment. The software engineer is being squeezed by the rest of the team. They’re usually asked to save everyone’s bacon. If something is not quite working in the electronics or mechanics, often you can work around it with a software kludge. -Mike And sometimes this reliance has catastrophic consequences. In 2019 over 300 people died in two 737 MAX airplane crashes. Investigation pinned this to a bug in the “Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System” (MCAS), one of the automated flight control systems. But Boeing only added MCAS in the first place to compensate for late-discovered issues with the plane’s aerodynamic profile. Rather than fix a trad issue with trad engineering, Boeing opted for the software kludge, and then people died. Constraints They have a [chip] time budget, you have a time budget, you say ‘I can’t quite make it. Do you have a little slop there? Can I get a fraction of a nanosecond?’ -Steve One implicit undercurrent in all the interviews was the notion of constraint. There are hard physical limits that their products needed to obey. It has to be light enough, or strong enough, or resistant enough, or run cool enough. There is a known quantity they have to maximize or minimize. Constraints are present in software, too. Code must fit in the memory of an embedded hardware device, the sensor needs a response in exactly 10 cycles, the API must stay under the rate limit. But constraints in software tend to be soft constraints. It is bad to go over them and the more we go over the worse it gets. We can slightly fudge the line if doing so will give us other benefits, like faster development time or simpler algorithms. In traditional engineering, most constraints are hard constraints. If the area of your box is a bit too wide then it won’t fit in the door.2 Sometimes this leads to unusual solutions. One time Carl’s team had to install a screw conveyor in an oil rig, then discovered it was just a couple inches too tall for the room. They couldn’t shrink the equipment, and they couldn’t raise the ceiling, since there were another four floors above it. The team’s solution? Cut a hole in the ceiling, put the equipment in, then put a box around the hole on the next floor so that nobody trips over it. Now that change is permanently part of the rig’s structure, something that has to be accommodated in every future change forever. And that leads to another difference: software engineers can undo their kludges. Trad engineers cannot. Do the differences make us special? While there are many ways we are different, there’s a difference between being “different” and being “special”. Yes, mechanical and electrical engineers don’t have to deal with the same security concerns we do. They also don’t have to deal with weather patterns to the same degree that civil engineers need to, and none of those three need to deal with the problems inherent in chemical engineering. Every field of engineering has unique challenges and software is no different. But they are all much more similar than they are different. Every field values upfront, abstract thinking, tidy work, and a good kludge in just the right place. Every field faces shifting requirements and unknown unknowns. Every field is siloed from the others: we know as little about the work of mechanical engineers as chemical engineers do. Many times in my interviews, people asked what the other fields of engineering were like. Nobody ever gets a chance to leave their bubble. And it’s a good thing that software isn’t special. It means that we can learn a lot on how to make software better from these other fields. And it means that they have a lot to learn from us. Because surprisingly, there are some ways that we are better at engineering than traditional engineers. Next time, we’ll cover what we can learn and what we can teach. Part three, What Engineering Can Teach (and Learn from) Us, is available here. If you enjoyed these essays, I have a weekly newsletter and am on Twitter. Thanks to Glenn Vanderburg, Chelsea Troy, Will Craft, and Dan Luu for feedback, and to all of the engineers whom I interviewed. They were not a crossover and so aren’t part of the interviews. [return] Some software follows hard constraints, too: if the printer skips a bit then your document is ruined. But “real-time computing” makes up a small minority of the software space. [return]

blocks.html_en: Debates about traditional versus software engineering revolve around what makes us different. The clichés here come from a different camp than the “what makes an engineer” clichés. The ways people try to define “engineering” often work to marginalize software. Differences like “we don’t have licenses” or “we’re not rigorous” are ways of saying that software is less prestigious, less “good” than traditional engineering. As we saw in the last essay, most of these don’t hold up, and the crossover engineers think the two jobs are much closer in nature than people who have only done one.

A good example of this is the NoEstimates movement: because estimates are difficult to make in software, supposedly unlike trad engineering, we should do away with them entirely.

blocks.html_en: As it’s told, Agile was a rejection of “Waterfall”, the old paradigm Winston Royce invented in 1970. Royce came up with the Waterfall model to mimic how “real” engineers built buildings. Waterfall says that you should do everything in a strict order, only progressing to the next stage of development when the current stage is completed. You only develop after you complete design, only test after you finish development, etc. This works for “real” engineering but utterly fails for software, where requirements change and often the customer doesn’t know what they want before you build it. So this is rejected by the Agile Manifesto in 2001, and everybody lived happily ever after.

blocks.html_en: Of course, this story is more fiction than fact. While Waterfall was a dominant model for some time, it was never quite as strict as we think it was today. Nor was it all that ubiquitous: most developers in the 70s and 80s were either working with an ad hoc plan or working in one of the many, many, many “incremental” models that were in fashion, like the Spiral Model and the V Model. Agile wasn’t a radical shift as much as a natural consequence of the trends at the time.

blocks.html_en: But all that is tangential to the core claim: software engineering is Agile, while trad engineering is Waterfall. And this, unsurprisingly, is a significant oversimplification.

blocks.html_en: It’s true that traditional engineers do a lot more upfront design and spend more time in dedicated testing than software engineers do. But this doesn’t mean they have Waterfall level rigidity, nor does it mean that our Agile is alien to them. Rather, spending a lot of time in phases is a natural consequence of the economic model. When iterations are longer and more expensive it makes more sense to spend more time planning them out. But people use “design” and “implement” in very different ways. When a civil engineer does a scale model, is that design or implementation? When an automotive engineer makes a full clay replica of a car to test its aesthetics and aerodynamics, is that design or implementation?

blocks.html_en: Why do we think software needs Agile and not Waterfall? Unpredictability. blocks.html_en: That’s from Nick Coghlan. I was surprised when he reached out for an interview; I knew about him as a core CPython developer. blocks.html_en: First of all, any less rigor we have isn’t entirely cultural, because the essential nature of software makes it a viable tradeoff. 这是跨界项目的第二部分。 第一部分在这里，第三部分在这里。 现在可以在此处查看基于这项工作的会议演讲。

没有人考虑在施工过程中移动桥梁的起点或终点。 -Justin Cave 我不得不移动一座桥。 -匿名1

卡尔担任机械验证工程师：他测试石油钻井平台以了解它们的振动程度。 人类长时间在石油钻井平台上工作和生活，如果振动太大，就可能无法入睡。 虽然钻机的设计目的是保持在阈值以下，但设计和最终版本常常存在分歧。

目前，他正在解释他们如何找到石油。 钻完一个洞后，他说，“你可能还想添加其他添加剂，比如酸或榛子壳，而且——”

我阻止了他。 “榛子壳？”

他笑了。 “你的储油库不像一个装满油的气球。 它更像是岩石中的多孔结构。” 钻孔时，管道中可能会突然失压。 这是极其危险的，因为你不知道自己是否已经闯入公海或刚刚进入局部空隙。 在后一种情况下，进一步挖掘并突然撞击高压区域可能会损坏管道。 通过泵入榛子壳，它们可以逐渐填充小空隙，并测试它们是否仍在结构中，如果仍在结构中，则逐渐平衡压力。

卡尔表示，石油公司是挪威榛子壳的最大买家。

关于传统工程与软件工程的争论围绕着我们的与众不同之处。 这里的陈词滥调与“工程师的成因”陈词滥调来自不同的阵营。 人们试图定义“工程”的方式往往会导致软件边缘化。 诸如“我们没有许可证”或“我们不严谨”之类的差异是在表达软件不如传统工程有声望、不如传统工程“好”。 正如我们在上一篇文章中看到的，其中大多数都站不住脚，跨界工程师认为这两项工作在本质上比只做过一项工作的人更接近。

相比之下，当人们谈论根本差异时，他们通常并不是要取消软件开发的合法性。 相反，隐含的重点是让软件变得“特殊”。 让软件成为狭隘的工程视角无法理解的东西。

我认为这是一种防御机制。 如果软件与传统如此不同，那么我们“不做工程师”也没关系。 当然，我们可以说，我们没有预先计划，但那是因为软件需求的变化比其他地方快得多。 我们不应用工程学，因为我们不应该应用工程学。 一个很好的例子就是“NoEstimates”运动：因为很难在软件中进行估算，据说与传统工程不同，所以我们应该完全废除它们。

这只有一个问题：作为软件工程师，我们深深误解了传统工程的本质。 我们并不特别。 几乎所有我们认为软件独特的东西都出现在工程的所有其他领域。 这样做的好处是——嗯，我们并不特别。 几乎所有我们认为软件糟糕的事情也是其他人都在努力解决的。

声称的差异

将“传统”（不同工程学科的总称）与软件进行比较是错误的。 大多数关于工程的争论都没有超出“软件与工程”的范围，或者将“工程”与土木工程混为一谈。 所有子领域都是不同的，一个领域的品质并不反映其他领域的品质。 经过几次采访后，我确定了一组“普遍”差异来讨论：

  1. 传统工程最好以瀑布方式完成，而软件最好以敏捷方式完成。
  2. 传统工程是非常可预测的，而软件是非常不可预测的。
  3. 工程主要是关于制造，而代码主要是关于设计，因为“代码就是设计”。
  4. 传统工程比软件工程严格得多。
  5. 软件的发展速度比传统工程快得多。

这些并不都是错的。 正如我们稍后将看到的，软件和传统之间绝对存在一些差异。 但大多数差异都是“错误的”，或者至少缺乏关键的细微差别。

传统是瀑布式，软件是敏捷式

如果我们认为有一件东西是独一无二的软件，那就是敏捷。

据说，敏捷是对“瀑布”的拒绝，“瀑布”是温斯顿·罗伊斯 (Winston Royce) 在 1970 年发明的旧范式。 罗伊斯提出了瀑布模型来模仿“真正的”工程师建造建筑物的方式。 瀑布说你应该严格按照顺序做每件事，只有当前阶段完成后才能进入下一阶段的开发。 只有在完成设计后才进行开发，只有在完成开发后才进行测试，等等。这适用于“真正的”工程，但对于软件来说完全失败，因为需求会发生变化，而且客户通常在构建之前并不知道他们想要什么。 所以这在 2001 年被敏捷宣言拒绝了，从此大家都过上了幸福的生活。

当然，这个故事更多的是虚构而非事实。 虽然瀑布模型曾一度占据主导地位，但它从来没有像我们今天想象的那么严格。 它也不是那么普遍：70 年代和 80 年代的大多数开发人员要么采用临时计划，要么采用许多、许多、许多流行的“增量”模型之一，例如螺旋模型和 V 模型。 敏捷并不是一种彻底的转变，而是当时趋势的自然结果。

但所有这些都与核心主张相悖：软件工程是敏捷，而传统工程是瀑布。 毫不奇怪，这是一种严重的过度简化。

确实，与软件工程师相比，传统工程师会进行更多的前期设计，并花费更多的时间进行专门测试。 但这并不意味着他们具有瀑布级别的刚性，也不意味着我们的敏捷对他们来说是陌生的。 相反，分阶段花费大量时间是经济模式的自然结果。 当迭代时间更长、成本更高时，花更多时间进行规划就更有意义。 但人们使用“设计”和“实施”的方式却截然不同。 当土木工程师制作比例模型时，是设计还是实施？ 当汽车工程师制作汽车的完整粘土复制品以测试其美学和空气动力学时，这是设计还是实施？

当涉及到制作电路板之类的事情时，第一次无法工作是很常见的。 你得重新做一次，你得把它送到工厂重新做一次。 你知道这会额外花费你 1000 英镑，并且还要多花两周的时间。 -迈克（电气）

我们在每个行业都看到了类似敏捷的创新。 如今，许多隧道都是采用奥地利隧道公司建造的，它依赖于迭代开发和大量的即兴创作空间。 工业工程手册强调交叉协作和快速的客户反馈。 即使是最具瀑布形式的工程（土木工程），一旦施工开始，也会逐渐转向更加敏捷的流程。 人们需要开放的沟通和适应来处理建筑中的实际问题。

为什么我们认为软件需要敏捷而不是瀑布？ 不可预测性。 只有当我们能够准确预测和估计项目中固有的障碍时，瀑布模型才有意义。 有人认为，由于软件是不可预测的，我们不能使用瀑布。 可能在计划进行到一半时，我们决定需要重新开始。 对于工程师来说有什么不同吗？ 他们的工作比我们的工作更可预测、更确定吗？

“软件更难以预测”

*笑声* - 道恩、马特、史蒂夫、迈克、马特、另一个马特

这种误解的部分原因在于我们看到的是工程过程的结果，而不是过程本身。 我们看不到因为有人向左建造了一英寸的墙，或者当关键供应商倒闭而发生的摩擦、超支和延误。 认为软件具有独特的不可预测性是一种特殊的傲慢。

另一部分来自于软件变化的速度。 感觉每一两年都会出现一种新的主​​导框架或语言，每个人都试图转向。 我们预计传统工程不会有同样不断变化的工具和范式。 在某种程度上，事实并非如此。 但减少客户流失并不等于没有客户流失，而且还有很多其他方式会导致事情变得不可预测。 一位芯片设计师史蒂夫发现这特别有趣：

在软件世界的环境中，人们正在思考“本月新的 JavaScript 捆绑程序是什么”。 在硬件世界中，问题是“本月硅晶圆厂的人员能为我们做什么”。 如果铸造厂有新的机器来制造芯片，你的计划就会改变。 不如图​​书馆那么快，但仍然相当快。 -史蒂夫（电气）

轶事太多，无法一一列举。 领土主张在建设过程中发生变化，严格的程序突然永久失败，新发现正在开发中。 一个人谈到了在桥梁基础上开始工作是多么令人沮丧，却发现这种特殊的土壤以一种奇怪的方式冻结，使其在地震中液化过多。 回到绘图板。

“代码就是设计”

“代码就是设计”是对那些认为“哦，如果我们只是用 UML 构建一个漂亮的模型，然后从 UML 自动生成所有代码，那么一切都会好起来”的人的反应。

这是尼克·科格伦发来的。 当他主动联系我接受采访时，我感到很惊讶。我知道他是一名 CPython 核心开发人员。 但在此之前，他是波音公司的系统集成工程师。 他称之为“系统架构的外交风格”。 波音公司将拥有多个独立的系统——在他的例子中，包括一架飞机、空中交通管制和一个天线阵列。 他必须与所有三个团队合作，以确保他们构建兼容的界面。 本质上是整合工作。 他认为“软件就是设计”是他以前的工作和现在的工作之间的根本区别。

其他人则不太确定。 “在我看来，”一位人士说道，“从 CPU 的第一个原理图到铸造厂推出的最终芯片，这一切都是设计”。 他们所有的时间都花在设计上，就像软件一样。 构建是最简单的部分：只需将设计交给代工厂并取回完成的芯片即可。

当然，芯片回来时会有缺陷，这意味着设计上的改变。 设计和构建并不像我们软件工程师想象的那么脱节。 许多机械工程师强烈地感受到了这一点。 建造的产品可能会显示出设计中的问题，也可能会显示出施工环境中的问题。 一位机械工程师迈克将其称为“修整”。 调整设计以处理施工过程中的轻微缺陷。 每一个建筑都会改变设计，设计也会改变建筑。

除此之外，还有一个问题：“设计”没有明确规定。 我们正在谈论架构概述吗？ 正式规范？ 详细的蓝图？ 如果代码就是设计，那么我们代码的正式规范是什么？ 对于复杂的项目，有许多不同类型、不同细节级别的设计。 如果你看一下桥梁平面图，你会发现有很多层分形细节。

我认为这是另一种情况，我们所说的设计和施工的含义在不同类型的工程之间确实有所不同。 是的，在土木工程中，施工阶段花费最多的时间和金钱，但这就是土木工程。 而且只有某些类型的土木工程，“桥梁和建筑物”才有效。 我们的刻板印象也是基于同样的工作。

我发现自己必须解释土木工程的许多方面你不会特别考虑。 […] 我告诉人们它指的是建造城市所需的任何东西。 -Jen（民事）

Rigor

软件中的制衡工作比传统工程多了 1,000,000 万倍。 […] 每当有人发推文时，比如 Excel 恐怖故事*笑声*我都会有令人惊叹的 Excel 恐怖故事 [...] 有时候，我很惊讶摩天大楼不会每天倒塌，飞机也不会坠毁。 -垫

人们说传统工程比软件严谨得多。 传统工程师根据第一原则仔细推理，而不是复制粘贴。 这通常表现为软件问题，我们需要对其进行更改才能成为“真正的”工程。 这也是错误的。

首先，我们所具有的任何不严格性并不完全是文化问题，因为软件的本质使其成为一种可行的权衡。 尼克将其解释为“验证假设”的差异：“到达某个点时，检查你的假设是否正确的最简单方法就是直接去做。” 软件让我们更容易地收集经验信息，这本身就是严谨的来源。

但关于严谨性的说法是基于软件的最终结果是不同的，即传统产品更加连贯，不那么草率。 那不是真的。 例如，我们保留更好的记录并使用更全面的验证。 我听过很多关于存储在 Excel 表格和旧文件柜中的关键信息的恐怖故事，这些信息变得过时和腐败。 为了得到我们视为既定的同样类型的自动化测试，很多人会不惜一切代价。

您可以随时添加更多括号。 -卡尔

真正的差异

那么软件与其他东西有何不同呢？ 有几种方法。

一致性

软件是完全综合的。 它完全受逻辑限制。 它不会像弹簧一样磨损，对吗？ 它只是做它应该做的事情。 实际上唯一可能出错的是规格。 该软件很糟糕。 -内森

软件比任何其他类型的工程都更加一致。 我们通常认为软件是一个巨大的混乱，相互依赖和不兼容的硬件的阴霾，但实际上我们的软件非常好。 如果我给你一个排序函数，你就可以期待它排序。 您不会期望它仅在 95% 的情况下对给定的（非病态）数字列表进行排序。 那太荒谬了。

相比之下，让我们看看物理材料。 在电气工程中，核心部件是电阻器：一根减少电流的电线。 电阻器以欧姆为单位进行测量，现成的商品电阻器的范围可以从一个欧姆到数亿欧姆。 许多商品电阻器都遵循色卡，以便轻松识别电阻：

因此，具有绿色、蓝色、红色的波段将具有 5600 欧姆。 但请注意最后一个带：它指定了容差。 颜色代码仅描述理论电阻：如果公差带为金色，则意味着电阻器的变化最多可达 5%。 如果您有一批 100 个这样的电阻器，有些是 5320 欧姆，有些是 5880 欧姆，了解哪个是哪个的唯一方法是单独测试每个电阻。 更不用说磨损或电阻如何随温度变化等。

所有物理材料都是如此。 在我开始这个项目之前，我在互联网上最喜欢的发现之一是 Fastenal 实验室页面。 Fastenal 生产螺丝。 他们的其中一页警告不要在铝板上使用不锈钢螺钉。

软件工程与此无关。

速度

该代码是硬件应如何运行的规范。 在传统工程中，我们必须做所有相同的工作来共享规范，但随后我们必须等待，让工厂或机械车间完成该死的东西的建造。 然后我们必须坐在那里自己安装或雇人安装。 然后我们必须对其进行几周的测试，看看它是否有效。 -哑光（化学）

这是无可辩驳的。 我们改变软件的速度比任何人改变系统的速度都要快得多。 几位工程师告诉我，改变有一个可量化的价格标签：每次你需要调整某些东西时，你都知道你会从预算中扣除 5000 美元。 而我可以更改一些代码并在几秒钟内运行所有测试。

我在其他领域发现最接近这一点的是化学工程。 “我早上会去看看昨晚出了什么问题，”前化学工程师拉贾说。 像一分钟周转这样的事情是闻所未闻的，而这已经是非软件工程最快的领域了。

这就是我们材料的本质。 这也是为什么其他工程领域通过创建这些设计工具和模拟逐渐使用更多软件的原因，工程师可以在实施之前使用软件对他们的想法进行原型设计。

这也有其阴暗的一面。 由于软件的迭代速度比 trad 更快，因此 trad 通常依靠软件来弥补物理设备的问题。

软件工程师正受到团队其他成员的挤压。 他们通常被要求保存每个人的培根。 如果电子或机械方面的某些功能不太正常，通常您可以通过软件组合来解决它。 -麦克风

有时这种依赖会带来灾难性的后果。 2019 年，两起 737 MAX 飞机失事造成 300 多人死亡。 调查将其归咎于自动飞行控制系统之一的“机动特性增强系统”（MCAS）中的一个错误。 但波音公司一开始只是添加了 MCAS，以弥补后来发现的飞机空气动力学问题。 波音没有用传统工程来解决传统问题，而是选择了软件拼凑，然后人们就死了。

约束条件

他们有一个[芯片]时间预算，你也有一个时间预算，你说‘我不太能做到。 你那里有一点斜坡吗？ 我能得到零点几纳秒吗？’-史蒂夫

所有访谈中隐含的一个暗流是约束的概念。 他们的产品需要遵守严格的物理限制。 它必须足够轻，或足够坚固，或足够耐用，或运行足够凉爽。 他们必须最大化或最小化已知的数量。

软件中也存在限制。 代码必须适合嵌入式硬件设备的内存，传感器需要在 10 个周期内准确响应，API 必须保持在速率限制以下。 但软件中的约束往往是软约束。 重复它们是不好的，而且我们越重复，情况就越糟糕。 如果这样做会给我们带来其他好处，例如更快的开发时间或更简单的算法，我们可以稍微捏造这条线。 在传统工程中，大多数约束都是硬约束。 如果盒子的面积有点太宽，那么它就装不进门。2

有时这会导致不寻常的解决方案。 有一次，卡尔的团队必须在石油钻井平台上安装螺旋输送机，然后发现它对于房间来说只高了几英寸。 他们无法缩小设备，也无法提高天花板，因为上面还有四层楼。 团队的解决方案？ 在天花板上挖一个洞，把设备放进去，然后在下一层的洞周围放一个盒子，这样就不会被绊倒了。 现在，这种变化已永久成为钻机结构的一部分，必须永远适应未来的每一次变化。 这导致了另一个区别：软件工程师可以消除他们的拼凑行为。 传统工程师不能。

这些差异让我们变得特别吗？

虽然我们有很多不同之处，但“不同”和“特殊”之间是有区别的。 是的，机械和电气工程师不必处理与我们相同的安全问题。 他们也不必像土木工程师那样处理天气模式，而且这三人都不需要处理化学工程固有的问题。 每个工程领域都有独特的挑战，软件也不例外。

但它们的相似之处远多于不同之处。 每个领域都重视提前、抽象思维、整洁的工作以及在正确的地方进行良好的整合。 每个领域都面临着不断变化的需求和未知的未知因素。 每个领域都与其他领域相互隔离：我们对机械工程师的工作知之甚少，就像对化学工程师的了解一样少。 在我的采访中，人们多次询问工程的其他领域是什么样的。 没有人有机会离开他们的泡沫。

幸运的是，软件并不特殊。 这意味着我们可以从这些其他领域学到很多关于如何使软件变得更好的知识。 这意味着他们有很多东西要向我们学习。 因为令人惊讶的是，在某些方面我们比传统工程师更擅长工程。 下一次，我们将讨论我们可以学到什么和可以教什么。
